5. **Separate blocking from non-blocking** — A point is blocking when the PR should not land until it is fixed: a correctness or security bug, a backward-compatibility break, a design problem that needs another look once addressed, an unaddressed maintainer comment, or anything a rule in this skill's files or an applicable `REVIEW.md` says always blocks or defaults to **Request Changes** (for example a non-exempt CI install, or a runner label that breaks the naming standard and no other CI uses). A performance regression on a hot path is blocking; a missing test is blocking only when the checklist or an applicable `REVIEW.md` requires that test. Everything else worth mentioning (naming, small refactors, consistency with nearby code, wording of comments and docs) is non-blocking: write "non-blocking" in it. Do not stretch a point to make it blocking.

## Directory Review Guides (`REVIEW.md`)

Any directory may contain a `REVIEW.md` with review rules for code under it. It applies to every changed file under that directory at any depth; for renames and deletions, check both the old and new paths.

```bash
gh api --paginate repos/pytorch/pytorch/issues/<PR_NUMBER>/comments
gh api --paginate repos/pytorch/pytorch/pulls/<PR_NUMBER>/reviews
gh api --paginate repos/pytorch/pytorch/pulls/<PR_NUMBER>/comments
gh api repos/pytorch/pytorch/collaborators/<LOGIN>/permission --jq .user.permissions
gh api repos/pytorch/pytorch/pulls/comments/<COMMENT_ID>/reactions
gh api repos/pytorch/pytorch/issues/comments/<COMMENT_ID>/reactions
```

5. List the `REVIEW.md` files that apply to each changed file (see "Directory Review Guides" above); leave reading them to sub-agents unless you review or fact-check a file yourself

Go through **every changed line** in the diff and evaluate it against the review checklist in [review-checklist.md](review-checklist.md).

When you have the Agent tool, whatever the PR's size, and unless the Time Budget's convergence or posting window is open (see "Time Budget"), spawn these reviewers in parallel, each over the full diff with the checklist's path and the `REVIEW.md` paths covering the changed files, with which files each one covers (Step 1, item 5), and each told to report every candidate problem with its `file:line` and evidence:

- **Tests:** how the PR's tests are written: tests that cannot fail or do not check what they claim, flakiness, and the checklist's Testing items. Whether the PR needs more tests is not a finding unless the checklist or an applicable `REVIEW.md` requires the test. A test the PR deletes without explaining why is a finding.
- **API and compatibility** (also give it [bc-guidelines.md](bc-guidelines.md)): public names, backward compatibility, docstrings, error messages, documentation.

Review every changed file covered by a `REVIEW.md` with its rules applied, including any rules they relax. With the fan-out, the reviewers above do this; without it, apply them yourself.

Evaluate BC implications per [bc-guidelines.md](bc-guidelines.md). For non-trivial BC questions, spawn a sub-agent to search for existing callers of the modified API.

Spawn the agents in parallel. Each independently verifies its findings by re-reading the relevant code and surrounding context (give each agent the paths of any `REVIEW.md` covering its findings' files), and returns **valid**, **invalid**, or **needs rewording** for each. On a re-review, a new blocking finding on covered code also needs rule 3's concrete failure (see "Re-reviews converge"); without one, it is non-blocking. Drop invalid issues, reword the rest. If unsure, leave the issue with a comment for the author that this is low confidence.

The Summary section is the one exception: it should briefly state what the PR does (1 sentence), list any applied `REVIEW.md` files, and then state the problems found, or explicitly say no issues were found.

files..agents/skills/pr-review/ci-dependencies:
This document covers package installs that run inside Linux CI jobs. Apply it whenever a PR changes code that runs in a Linux CI build or test job: anything under `.ci/` other than `.ci/docker/`, anything under `.github/`, and scripts those jobs run, such as `benchmarks/dynamo/` and `test/`.

The fix is to add the package to the CI image: `.ci/docker/requirements-ci.txt`, or a script under `.ci/docker/common/`. Pin it there with `==`: upgrades then come through a PR that bumps the pin, which rebuilds the image and runs CI on it. An exact `==` pin at the install site is not a fix, because the package's own dependencies still resolve fresh on every run.

Adding a package to `requirements-ci.txt` is the fix even though some jobs still resolve it on each run: s390x installs that file at test time into an image that doesn't preinstall it, and macOS and Windows have no image.

When the changed dependency is used only by workflows that don't run on PRs by default, ask for a representative ciflow label that exercises it (for example `ciflow/inductor-periodic` for a benchmark-only dependency). Check the PR's labels first (`labels` from `gh pr view`) and do not ask for one that is already applied; if the labels are not available (GitHub Actions mode does not provide them, and Local Branch mode has no PR), ask for the label and say it may already be applied. A label covers only the workflows its tag triggers: `ciflow/docker` does not exercise a benchmark-only dependency. A shared change, such as to `requirements-ci.txt` or a base Dockerfile, does not by itself call for every consumer workflow's label; the image builds are already exercised by `ciflow/docker`.

- Jobs not run on an image built with `requirements-ci.txt`.

- [ ] **Cross-stream tensor lifetime / recordStream** — PR uses a tensor on a stream other than the one it was allocated on. Check that either the side-stream use is synced back to the creation stream before the last reference is dropped, or `record_stream()` / `recordStream()` is called; with neither, the allocator may reuse the memory while the side stream is still using it. If the PR adds `record_stream`, don't flag it automatically: decide whether it is avoidable, using the `cuda-streams` skill (`../cuda-streams/SKILL.md`), and say which case you think applies and why

- [ ] **elementwise_dtypes / TensorIterator** — PR manually implements type promotion logic for elementwise ops. In Python, use `elementwise_dtypes()` from `torch/_prims_common/` with the appropriate `ELEMENTWISE_TYPE_PROMOTION_KIND`. In C++, use `TensorIteratorConfig` which handles type promotion automatically: call `.promote_inputs_to_common_dtype(true)` and `.cast_common_dtype_to_outputs(true)` on the config builder, then `TensorIterator` computes `common_dtype()` for the kernel and handles all input/output casting. Kernels should operate on `iter.common_dtype()` via `AT_DISPATCH` rather than manually checking and promoting dtypes

- [ ] **Complex dtype handling** — PR manually maps between complex and real dtypes (e.g., `complex64` to `float32`) instead of using `corresponding_real_dtype()` / `corresponding_complex_dtype()` from `torch/_prims_common/`

- [ ] **safe_globals** — Calling `torch.serialization.add_safe_globals()` is NEVER OK outside `torch/serialization.py` and `torch/_weights_only_unpickler.py`; Request Changes on any new call and never suggest it. Any new allowlisted global must pass the review in `torch/REVIEW.md`, even when the changed file is outside `torch/`

- [ ] **Runner naming standard** — PR adds or changes a runner label, or adds CI that inherits one from an input, matrix or dispatch default or option, and the label breaks the runner naming standard in [ci-runner-naming.md](ci-runner-naming.md). If no other CI in this repo uses that label, this always means **Request Changes**; if other CI already uses it, give a short non-blocking heads-up instead

When a PR changes code that runs in a Linux CI build or test job (anything under `.ci/` other than `.ci/docker/`, `.github/`, or scripts those jobs run, such as `benchmarks/dynamo/` and `test/`):

- [ ] **No package resolution at test time** — PR adds an install that resolves packages from an index while a Linux CI job runs, instead of adding them to the CI image. Apply [ci-dependencies.md](ci-dependencies.md) for what counts, the fix, and the exemptions. A non-exempt install always means **Request Changes**

- [ ] **Third-party code pinned by commit SHA** - Pin dependencies (submodules, script clones/checkouts, `pip install git+`, pin files, Actions `uses:`) by full commit SHA, never mutable tags, branches, or no ref at all (first-party `pytorch/*` repos, including Actions refs and script clones, are exempt). Use the commit an upstream release tag points to (the `^{}` commit for annotated tags) and note the tag name. Shell scripts in `.ci/pytorch` read the SHA from `.github/ci_commit_pins/<repo>.txt` via `get_pinned_commit`, with the tag noted at the call site; other scripts may inline the SHA with a tag comment. Nightly pin bumps via `update-commit-hashes` in `.github/workflows/nightly.yml` are fine; do not add dependencies whose consumers the bump PR's CI does not exercise (e.g. schedule-only consumers), leaving bot-merged bumps untested; bump those by hand in reviewed PRs

a pass must not eliminate `x.clone()`, by the same rule as in [Altering Aliasing](#altering-aliasing): passes must neither introduce nor remove aliasing between user-visible inputs and outputs.

  Note: [#198735](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/pull/198735) will relax the "introduce" half of this rule for forward and inference graphs. AOTAutograd records which user inputs and outputs share a storage in eager (`ViewAndMutationMeta.aliased_input_output_pairs` and `aliased_output_pairs`). When lowering the output node, Inductor compares these with the buffers the user-visible outputs actually use, and copies any output that has a new input-output or output-output alias, keeping its original strides. Once it lands, introducing such an alias costs a copy but is not a correctness bug. Two constraints remain: removing an eager alias is not repaired, and the repair copy is made at the output, after input mutations, so passes must still preserve the values observed across mutations (see [Mutations](#mutations)).
